newsitem.title: GERMANY: German grain sellers wary of price strength.
newsitem.headline: German grain sellers wary of price strength.

text.p: Rising prices on world markets may deter buyers in negotiations over new crop supplies, traders attending an industry gathering said.
"Because of the drought fears in Western Europe, our new crop wheat offers are at par with remaining old crop quantities, where high holding costs are included," an export broker said.
"We think this is dangerous because we won't attract consumers at that level," he added.
"Only speculative trade buyers are in the market and they may find prices will fall later on grain area expansions."
Some 450 traders and consumers were gathering for the Hamburg Grain and Feeds Association's April exchange, which serves as a forum for informal pre-harvest discussions.
They said buyers were also cautious because they believed strong internal grain prices would discourage subsidised EU exports, which might add to a high carry-over into the 1997/98 season.
They were hoping for price falls ahead of and during the 1997 harvest.

But Christof Buchholz, managing director of the Hamburg trade association, said the pace of EU grain and flour export licence awards this season had been rapid, and export availability of EU grain may be lower than previously thought.
"EU grain intervention stocks are nearing just 1.9 million tonnes, of which 90 percent are in Germany, and analysts wonder where some of the massive 1996 harvest has ended up," he said.
"Some may have been fed directly on farms...grain feeding has rising sharply because of high substitute prices."
Export brokers were quoting bread wheat with 12 percent protein at 282.50 marks fob, basis first half September.
This was up five marks on last week and identical with the April old crop price, basis a 3,000 tonne shipment fob Baltic.
Barley and rye prices were also around 2.50 marks up on last week, with barley in a 265-290 marks fob range and rye at around 260-270, but buyers were mostly passive.
Grain prices elsewhere in Europe have risen more sharply over the past few trading days on fears of drought damage to crops in France, Spain, Britain and Denmark.
In France, prices for the new crop rose up to three percent on Monday.
The EU, in response to the surge, reduced its zero daily refund for wheat to zero, making it harder for traders to use the EU's daily channel for wheat exports.
U.S. weather also fuelled concern in the French market. Chicago May wheat futures on Monday jumped to seven-month highs on fears of winterkill in the hard red winter wheat belt.
By comparison, German grain crops looked fairly healthy and -- given an increase in the overall area for 1997 -- likely to exceed last year's record 42.1 million tonnes.
The weather had been slightly cold, but not too dry.
Meals and feeds brokers said their customers were unwilling to commit to long-term dates because of the heavily fluctuating Chicago soy complex and the strong dollar.
"Feed manufacturers still need plenty of protein meals for the second half of 1997, but baulk at high prices," one said.
"We're counting the days until the arrival of Latin American soy crops."
